chunk_text:
Mastering Kubernetes Autoscaling for AI and Real-Time Traffic

Autoscaling Kubernetes for real-time traffic, complex workloads, and AI/LLM applications introduces unique performance and scalability challenges. This session focuses on practical methods to scale efficiently for latency-sensitive scenarios and resource-intensive AI-driven tasks. We’ll explore Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling (KEDA) strategies tailored specifically for dynamic real-time traffic, custom metrics for AI workloads, and considerations for managing complex services. Additionally, we’ll address the trade-offs involved, pitfalls to avoid, and illustrate best practices through real-world examples. Join us for an insightful look at building robust autoscaling strategies optimized for real-time responsiveness, AI efficiency, and cost control in Kubernetes.

name: Autoscaling Challenges on Kubernetes
chunk_text:
Autoscaling Challenges on Kubernetes

Autoscaling on Kubernetes can save costs, boost performance, and streamline operations - but only if done right. In this session, we’ll explore the real-world challenges of autoscaling containerized workloads, from unpredictable traffic patterns to complex resource management across multiple services. We’ll dive into how Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling (KEDA) can simplify your scaling logic with custom metrics and various triggers, so you can handle spikes efficiently without overprovisioning. We’ll cover resource-based, event driven, custom metrics based and HTTP-driven scaling, and the often-overlooked scale-to-zero strategy - helping you optimize for both capacity and cost. To bring these concepts to life, we’ll walk through a live demo showing how to set up and monitor diverse scaling scenarios in real time. Get ready to tackle the pitfalls of autoscaling head-on and deploy robust, cost-effective solutions in your own Kubernetes environment.

chunk_text: This is why we should do autoscaling and what are the types of autoscaling. With ScaledObject, we can target any Deployment, StatefulSet, or any custom resource that implements scale sub-resource. For example, Argo Rollouts, we can also target them. chunk_text: Then we define the minimum and maximum replicas, a bunch of additional configuration that's not present here, and then the trigger section. Are there any users of KEDA in the audience? I have a bunch of people. Is there anyone who hasn't heard about KEDA before? A few people. The second type of autoscaling on Kubernetes is Kubernetes jobs. Instead of scaling out horizontally the workloads, we can also schedule Kubernetes jobs based on the very same events. For example, there are 5 messages in the Kafka topic, so let's start 5 Kubernetes jobs. Why is it good? If you think about horizontal scaling and how we scale it based on external metrics, what could happen if the workload takes the data and processes it for a very long time? It could be minutes, maybe hours, maybe days. The workload consumes the particular event. Then under the HPA, Kubernetes might think that the application should already be scaled to a lower amount of replicas, so it will try to kill the pod. For this case, it's much better to actually use Kubernetes jobs, and in this particular case it's ScaleJob. You can think of it as a CronJob on steroids. CronJob allows you to specify a cron schedule and based on the schedule you can create those Kubernetes jobs that process the work and finish. With ScaleJobs, we have the flexibility that we can define external triggers. For example, the very same RabbitMQ, we can say 10 messages in RabbitMQ, we will spin 10 ScaleJobs, they will process the work independently along each execution, and then it's done. This is the second type of major workloads with KEDA.

name: Mastering Kubernetes Autoscaling for AI and Real-Time Traffic
chunk_text: Cron scaler allows you to scale based on the specific current schedule. There are users that would like to scale to 0 outside of working hours. The recommendation is to not use the cron scaler to 0, but to use it vice versa. So in the min replica section specify 0 and then in the cron section specify when we would like to be on top of it, so specify the working hours. This is very specific to KEDA but very important. Another thing with KEDA is we are importing the external systems, and we can easily overload the external system. For example, if we are getting Prometheus metrics, we can overload Prometheus because we are sending way too many requests. Always make sure to configure in the scaled object the polling properly. For the 1 to 1 scaling, this is handled by HPA, so we should be careful about that. This one is maybe a little bit controversial because with KEDA, the very typical setup is you have a Kubernetes cluster, you have already Prometheus in the Kubernetes cluster, and you would like to start scaling out, you would like to start the application autoscaling. The very typical scenario is that you will start with Prometheus scaler. There is a scaler in KEDA that can talk to Prometheus and evaluate the query, and based on the query it can do the scaling. This is a very good scenario. It's very useful, but there are some problems with this setup. For small workloads or low traffic applications, it's a very good solution. I know about users when they actually just deployed Kubernetes and just deployed Prometheus cluster for the autoscaling itself. There are a bunch of problems with this setup. Why? If you look at this diagram, we have KEDA which drives the autoscaling, we have the blue section which is the workload, and then we have Prometheus, Datadog, Dynatrace, whatever metric solution. What do we need to do? First, we need to scrape the particular metric from the workload to Prometheus, and then back scrape it to KEDA and do the final decision. If the traffic is very time sensitive, more like the HTTP traffic, what users usually do is they try to reuse those scraping periods to a very minimum. If you are at a certain scale, you have a lot of services talking to Kubernetes, a lot of queries, and Prometheus might go down or start complaining about this kind of stuff. You might get outages if you are using, for example, Datadog. You might be rate limited because you send way too many requests to the Datadog API basically every second asking about hundreds of resources. This might also be pricey because you are sending a lot of traffic out of the cluster and back because usually if you have a hosted solution you are sending a lot of stuff. Be careful about this setup. If you are running it and you are happy with it, it's good, but after you hit some certain scale, this might be very problematic. The solution is to try to get the metrics directly from the workload, not use intermediate solutions, which is more real time, and you don't overload the actual monitoring tool.

chunk_text: This is another problem. If you have a lot of objects going to the same server, you can overload it. Be careful when you are designing autoscaling operators because you cannot just start with simple stuff, just autoscale these applications. You need to think about the consequences because you usually have a chain of microservices or chain of applications connected together. If you scale one of them, the problem might happen in another one. What's next for the whole autoscaling story? I would like to recap why autoscaling is important. You need to configure both cluster level autoscaling. If you are running on AWS, for example, it's Karpenter or cluster autoscaler, and application level autoscaling, because application level autoscaling is making the pressure on cluster level autoscaling. As you are adding more pods, the cluster autoscaler is adding more Kubernetes nodes. You should really think about configuring both layers together. With horizontal scaling, there are some problems that even if you are trying to get real-time traffic, real-time metrics, and scale out as soon as you get the metrics, this might be too late. For example, if your applications are slow to start, for example, Python or Java applications that require a lot of time to warm up and start, even real-time scaling might not be enough because you are adding more replicas, but the application is not ready itself. Another idea is to use predictive scaling. What does it mean? We are getting all the different metrics from different systems, different workloads, and we can use some time series models to spot the trends. For example, if your workload has seasonality traffic or periodic traffic, it's a very good idea to do this kind of stuff, and then you can combine predictive scaling with traditional scaling and scale a few minutes ahead of the actual load so you give time for the application to properly prepare. On this graph, the blue part, the left part is the actual metrics that we are getting like this nice wave, and the purple line, which is not so visible here, is the actual prediction. We got the prediction from this actual data, so this is from the actual workload running there. Predictive scaling is something to go ahead of the problems with cold start. This is a good idea to do. The additional problem with autoscaling applications is the stateful workloads. All the stuff we mentioned was aimed towards stateless workloads, so applications that are cloud native ready, meaning they are able to start very early. They are like, let's say small as possible, the container will be pulled very quickly on the node and scaled out, but there are still four workloads that need to manage the state somehow. This is one of the topics that needs to be tackled over the coming months or years. This is the next topic for autoscaling: how to deal with managing the state and autoscaling itself as well.

By its nature, HTTP traffic is very sensitive to time because there are delays or timeouts on the HTTP configuration on the client side. We need to be sure to scale out very fast in order to process all the requests coming to our application. Luckily, we can also do this kind of stuff. HTTP traffic is also an event, so we should be able to autoscale it. I talk about the challenges, the push versus pull model, where we are not pulling the data, but we need to push the data to the application, so we need to be very fast. We need to be close to real time in order to serve all the requests. There are a lot of other challenges: there is gRPC traffic, WebSockets, TLS, header-based traffic. Also, maybe scale to zero would be nice with this approach.

chunk_text: If we look at this diagram on the left-hand side, there is a picture where we can see the yellow part. This represents the number of resources that we have. Sometimes we are underprovisioned. This means latency is bad, and overall, something we would like to avoid. The overprovisioning means that we are spending way too much money for the stuff we don't need. The ideal case is to get somewhere close to the image on the right-hand side where the number or the amount of resources reflects the actual need for our solution. These are just the two aspects why we should care about autoscaling. The main two aspects are cost reduction, so we can really save a huge amount of resources. The numbers mentioned there are not made up. This is from my experience over the years. I can see that people are able to save 30 or 40%, sometimes even 60%, but it was like an extreme situation when the application and the whole environment was built around, I believe it was Kafka, so some event-driven asynchronous system, and when we plug autoscaling in, they were able to scale out those microservices only based on demand. The 30 or 40% is something you can really achieve. The second aspect and also very important is the performance. Because you can specify your resources. You can say, OK, I don't need autoscaling because we have way too many resources and we have stable workload. But there are cases where you have some sudden spikes of traffic and even your refined resources are not able to handle the load. One of the examples, recently I talked to an American bank. They have this kind of issue when they have a series of microservices, they autoscale them just based on the CPU or memory consumption. We will cover this later on, but this scaling is very slow and for majority of time it was working for them very well. These microservices were, I believe, taking care of some payment processing. Then there was some sudden event happening, and there were a lot of users of this particular application trying to do payments, and those microservices weren't able to catch up and scale out properly. It resulted in a really bad situation for them because they weren't able to catch those sudden traffic spikes. This is why we do need autoscaling.

name: Autoscaling Challenges on Kubernetes
chunk_text: Now let's talk about the challenges with autoscaling because this is important. First, if there are some KEDA users, this is a very typical use case with KEDA. When you use Prometheus, Datadog, Dynatrace, or any monitoring solution to collect metrics from your applications or whatever you have deployed in the Kubernetes cluster, you have these metrics. You say, okay, I have these metrics already in Prometheus, so let's create them and scale based on that. It works for a lot of cases, but there are some challenges because there is an intermediate component, the Prometheus server. What we need to do is first scrape the metrics from the application, then scrape the metrics from Prometheus to KEDA. This could be based on the configuration, it could be around maybe 40 seconds, one minute. It depends on the configuration of your setup. And for a lot of cases, this is okay because you are using some average. Minutes or two is okay too, but if you need more closer to real-time stuff, this gets tricky. First thing that users typically do, they reuse the scraping periods both on the application. So from the application to Prometheus and also from KEDA. This works for a lot of cases, but again, it introduces some problems because we can overload the Prometheus instance, for example. If you have your Prometheus instance that you manage, or your infra team or monitoring team is managing Prometheus, if you reduce the polling interval, you can really overload Prometheus, because what it does under the hood is it periodically asks Prometheus, give me the latest metric, give me the latest metric. If we reuse this scraping period, for example, to two seconds, five seconds, we send a lot of data to Prometheus, especially if we are operating at larger scale. So we have a lot of applications. This is a common question we hear from users. I see these timeouts in KEDA because we are not getting the metrics from Prometheus. This is the reason. Another challenge with that is, for example, if you have multiple clusters across multiple availability zones, and Prometheus is in one zone and the cluster is in another availability zone, you can introduce a lot of traffic going back and forth between the Kubernetes cluster and Prometheus, which might be costly.

name: Autoscaling Challenges on Kubernetes
chunk_text: If you start scaling out some part of your infrastructure, always think about, okay, this could also cause problems in my database. So you should scale it out as well, which is more tricky because scaling out stateful workloads is more critical, or you can try to reduce some kind of load by stuff like that. The other thing is all the stuff we discussed here was horizontal scaling. Horizontal scaling is adding more replicas of the very same application based on the metrics. There is a rule that if you are using HPA or KEDA and you are scaling based on CPU or memory metrics, you shouldn't mix it with VPA, vertical pod autoscale, which is also available in Kubernetes. Vertical pod autoscale does the thing that it can resize your workload based on the metrics, so it can give it more resources or less. If you use the same HPA and VPA at the same time for the same workload, HPA will try to scale it out, for example, add more replicas, and VPA at the same time will try to resize it. This is not a good thing. Another thing with vertical scaling is that sometimes vertical autoscaling is good for right-sizing. This is where I suggest to use VPA in combination, not to actually modify the resources, but just give you recommendations. Okay, you should probably size this workload this way. But sometimes scaling is not just about right-sizing. For example, you have a legacy application written in Python or Java, and for start, it needs a lot of memory. It needs to download all the dependencies from the internet, it needs to start the JVM and all this kind of stuff. You know that for the start of the container, you need, for example, two gigabytes of memory, but once the application is started, you know that it can safely work with 500 megabytes of memory. With VPA, you cannot do this because VPA will try to always optimize over some average. It'll try to find a balance between those two values, and it'll probably stick to the two gigabytes for the whole lifetime of the pod. Luckily, there's a solution with the recent Kubernetes version, which is 1.23. There is a new feature added as beta; it was alpha before, so behind feature gate, and it's called in-place pod resize. What it does, as the name says, it allows you to resize your containers or pods in your Kubernetes cluster in time without any disruptions or restarts. You can basically say, okay, give this container more resources or less. For that, we developed this simple feature called pod resource profile, where you can target some workloads and specify some conditions.

name: Autoscaling Challenges on Kubernetes
chunk_text: Another challenge with autoscaling is, okay, I have my database, for example, it could be a database on top, and we have a lot of consumers accessing the same database, and we are scaling them out based on some metrics. This is perfect. But what happens if all of these workloads scale out to maximum at the same time? Especially if you are managing the database or the service yourself, it is not some hosted service in AWS, you can easily overload the database. So you should be careful about properly configuring the individual scaled objects because each scaled object would be defined, for example, to scale to 10 replicas. In total, it could be 40, but you know that your application can handle only 20. So you would like to reduce that. We have a way to do that. We can specify what we call a scaling group. In the scaling group, you can define dynamic rules to specify, okay, this group of objects can in total scale out to, for example, 100 replicas. We try to maintain the number of replicas across this workload. This is important to think about with downstream services.

Autoscaling on Kubernetes can save costs, boost performance, and streamline operations - but only if done right. In this session, we’ll explore the real-world challenges of autoscaling containerized workloads, from unpredictable traffic patterns to complex resource management across multiple services. We’ll dive into how Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling (KEDA) can simplify your scaling logic with custom metrics and various triggers, so you can handle spikes efficiently without overprovisioning. We’ll cover resource-based, event driven, custom metrics based and HTTP-driven scaling, and the often-overlooked scale-to-zero strategy - helping you optimize for both capacity and cost. To bring these concepts to life, we’ll walk through a live demo showing how to set up and monitor diverse scaling scenarios in real time. Get ready to tackle the pitfalls of autoscaling head-on and deploy robust, cost-effective solutions in your own Kubernetes environment.

The slide highlights the limitations of relying solely on horizontal scaling in Kubernetes, distinguishing between Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA). Horizontal scaling adds more replicas based on metrics like CPU or memory, while vertical scaling adjusts resource allocation per pod. However, using HPA and VPA simultaneously on the same workload can cause conflicts, as HPA scales out pods and VPA resizes them concurrently. Vertical autoscaling is often best suited for right-sizing workloads rather than dynamic resizing. Some applications, such as those written in Python or Java, require high memory during startup to load dependencies or initialize the JVM but need significantly less memory afterward. VPA tends to optimize for an average resource need, often maintaining higher allocations throughout the pod's lifetime, which is inefficient. This underscores the importance of understanding application-specific resource patterns and carefully choosing autoscaling strategies beyond simple horizontal scaling to optimize resource use effectively.

Custom metrics collection for autoscaling often relies on intermediate metrics scrapers and storage solutions like Prometheus, Datadog, and Dynatrace, as well as cloud provider platforms such as GCP, AWS, and Azure. While these tools enable scaling based on existing metrics, they introduce several challenges. Reducing scraping intervals to achieve near real-time scaling risks overloading the metrics store, leading to timeouts and degraded performance. Additionally, when clusters and metrics stores reside in different availability zones, the resulting zone-to-zone traffic increases operational costs. Managing this extra component adds complexity and overhead, highlighting the trade-offs between leveraging established monitoring platforms and the responsiveness and cost-efficiency of autoscaling solutions.

Horizontal autoscaling in Kubernetes can be implemented through three main approaches: Resource Based, Reactive, and Proactive autoscaling. However, this method may not always reflect actual workload demands, especially when resource usage is low but processing needs are high. Reactive autoscaling addresses this by scaling in response to real-time external signals such as HTTP request rates or Kafka consumer lag, dynamically adjusting to current demand. Proactive autoscaling anticipates future load by analyzing metrics like Kafka producer rates, enabling the system to scale up before demand peaks. This approach improves processing latency and throughput without increasing overall costs, as scaling duration is optimized. Tools like KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) facilitate reactive and proactive autoscaling by integrating custom metrics and event sources into Kubernetes scaling decisions, enhancing responsiveness and efficiency in diverse workload scenarios.

The architecture outlines how KEDA integrates with a Kubernetes cluster to enable event-driven autoscaling. At the core, KEDA acts as an intermediary layer between an external trigger source and the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). The process begins with a ScaledObject, which registers scaling definitions and trigger configurations with the Kubernetes API Server. These definitions tell KEDA what metrics or events to listen for when deciding to scale workloads.

Inside KEDA, three main components work together: the Metrics adapter, Controller, and Scaler. The Metrics adapter translates external event metrics into a format understandable by Kubernetes. The Controller monitors the state and orchestrates scaling decisions, while the Scaler connects directly to the external trigger source to detect relevant events. When an event occurs—such as a message in a queue or an HTTP request spike—the Scaler informs the Controller, which then signals the Metrics adapter to update metrics for the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.

The HPA responds by adjusting the number of workload pods, scaling up when there are one or more active events and scaling down when events cease. The arrows and annotations clarify state transitions—like scaling from zero to one pod or from multiple pods down to one—highlighting KEDA’s ability to handle scale-to-zero scenarios efficiently. This architecture is significant because it enables Kubernetes workloads to scale dynamically based on external, event-driven triggers rather than just internal resource metrics, improving responsiveness and resource optimization.

Kubernetes bietet mit dem Horizontal Pod Autoscaler die Möglichkeit, auf Basis von CPU- oder RAM-Auslastung die Anzahl der laufenden Applikationsinstanzen zu verändern. Allerdings sind moderne Anwendungen oftmals von einer Vielzahl von Komponenten abhängig und müssen auf externe Ereignisse reagieren können. KEDA bietet dafür eine einfache und flexible Lösung.

Autoskalierung ist eine meiner Lieblingsfunktionen von Kubernetes. Der Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) ist ein Built-in-Feature von Kubernetes, das Pods basierend auf der CPU- oder RAM-Auslastung skalieren kann. Das ist ein guter Anfang für moderne Applikationen, aber vor allem bei verteilten Anwendungen hat man oft mehrere Komponenten bzw. Abhängigkeiten außerhalb des Kubernetes-Clusters. Das kann ein Azure Service Bus, eine Cassandra Datenbank, MongoDB oder Elasticsearch sein. Mit dem HPA können diese Bedürfnisse nicht erfüllt werden, da die Pods nicht anhand der Metriken dieser Komponenten skaliert werden können. An dieser Stelle kommt KEDA [1] ins Spiel.

Mit KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling), der ereignisgesteuerten Autoskalierung von Kubernetes, können ganz einfach vorgefertigte Scaler in einen bestehenden Kubernetes-Cluster integriert werden. Diese Scaler überwachen die konfigurierten externen Quellen und skalieren die Pods der Anwendung entsprechend.

Ein praktisches Beispiel wäre ein Onlineshop am Black Friday, der hunderte oder tausende Bestellungen entgegennimmt. Diese Bestellungen werden in einer Queue gespeichert und dann verarbeitet. Die Anwendung, die die Nachrichten verarbeitet, sollte in diesem Fall mit KEDA skaliert werden, um eine zeitnahe Verarbeitung aller Bestellungen gewährleisten zu können.

Kubernetes bietet mit dem Horizontal Pod Autoscaler die Möglichkeit, auf Basis von CPU- oder RAM-Auslastung die Anzahl der laufenden Applikationsinstanzen zu verändern. Allerdings sind moderne Anwendungen oftmals von einer Vielzahl von Komponenten abhängig und müssen auf externe Ereignisse reagieren können. KEDA bietet dafür eine einfache und flexible Lösung.
